subChunks.title: Choosing the Right Data Type
subChunks.hookHtml: The type you assign to a column determines what the database stores, how much space it uses, and what operations are valid. Wrong types cause subtle bugs and wasted storage.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Core types (standard SQL)

TypeUse forExample
INTEGER / INTWhole numbersid, count, xp
BIGINTVery large whole numbersUnix timestamps, row counts > 2 billion
DECIMAL(p,s) / NUMERIC(p,s)Exact decimal numbers (p=total digits, s=decimal places)price DECIMAL(10,2)
REAL / FLOATApproximate floating-pointScientific measurements
TEXT / VARCHAR(n)Variable-length textname, email, description
CHAR(n)Fixed-length text, padded to nISO country codes
BOOLEANTrue/false valuesis_active, is_verified
DATEDate without timejoined_date
TIMESTAMPDate + timecreated_at, updated_at
BLOB / BYTEABinary dataFile contents, images

Money: use DECIMAL, never FLOAT

FLOAT is an approximation. 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 in floating point. For money, use DECIMAL(10,2) for exact cents.

Enums

-- PostgreSQL:
CREATE TYPE difficulty AS ENUM ('Easy', 'Medium', 'Hard', 'Expert');

-- Most engines: use a CHECK constraint instead:
difficulty TEXT CHECK (difficulty IN ('Easy','Medium','Hard','Expert'))

SQLite's type flexibility

SQLite uses dynamic typing — any value can go in any column. This is convenient for learning but not representative of PostgreSQL/MySQL behaviour. In production, type enforcement matters.

storyBeats.text: The Archivist traces the type column header. 'This one detail affects everything downstream.'

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Use DECIMAL for money — never FLOAT. Floating-point arithmetic is approximate by design. Use TEXT or VARCHAR for variable strings. Use TIMESTAMP for any date with time. The right type prevents whole categories of bug before you write a single query.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Schema design critique

Below is a flawed schema. Identify the type errors and explain the correct fix for each:

CREATE TABLE payments (
  id          TEXT    PRIMARY KEY,  -- (1)
  amount      FLOAT   NOT NULL,     -- (2)
  created_at  TEXT    NOT NULL,     -- (3)
  is_refunded INTEGER NOT NULL      -- (4)
);
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) `id TEXT` — Using TEXT for a primary key is valid but unusual. If auto-incrementing IDs are desired, use INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (SQLite) or SERIAL/BIGSERIAL (PostgreSQL). UUIDs as TEXT are fine.

(2) `amount FLOAT` — Critical error for financial data. FLOAT is approximate; 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3 exactly. Use DECIMAL(10,2) or INTEGER (storing cents, e.g. 1099 for £10.99).

(3) `created_at TEXT` — Technically works in SQLite if ISO 8601 format is enforced. In PostgreSQL/MySQL, use TIMESTAMP or TIMESTAMPTZ for proper date/time operations and timezone support.

(4) `is_refunded INTEGER` — Storing booleans as integers works (0/1) but obscures intent. Use BOOLEAN (PostgreSQL/MySQL) or CHECK(is_refunded IN (0,1)) for clarity.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Write a CREATE TABLE statement for an orders table with proper types for: order ID (auto-increment), customer name (text, required), total price (exact decimal, 2 places, required), ordered at (timestamp, required), is_shipped (boolean, default false).
subChunks.modelAnswer:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          INTEGER      PRIMARY KEY,  -- auto-increment in SQLite
  customer    TEXT         NOT NULL,
  total_price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
  ordered_at  TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
  is_shipped  BOOLEAN      NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE
);
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why FLOAT is wrong for storing money in a database and what type to use instead. Give a concrete example of a bug FLOAT causes.

questions.prompt: Which type should you use to store a price like £10.99?
questions.explanation: DECIMAL stores exact decimal values. FLOAT is an approximation — 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 in binary float, which causes incorrect totals when summing prices.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between VARCHAR(100) and TEXT?
options: VARCHAR(100) limits the value to 100 characters; TEXT has no engine-enforced character limit
TEXT stores only ASCII; VARCHAR supports Unicode
VARCHAR is faster; TEXT is for large documents only
They are identical in all engines
questions.answer: VARCHAR(100) limits the value to 100 characters; TEXT has no engine-enforced character limit
questions.explanation: VARCHAR(n) enforces a maximum length — the engine rejects longer values. TEXT typically allows up to engine-specific maximums (often GB). In PostgreSQL there is essentially no performance difference between them.

questions.prompt: When should you use BIGINT instead of INTEGER?
options: When values may exceed ~2.1 billion (the 32-bit signed integer limit)
BIGINT and INTEGER are the same in SQL
questions.answer: When values may exceed ~2.1 billion (the 32-bit signed integer limit)
questions.explanation: INTEGER (32-bit) holds approximately -2.1B to 2.1B. BIGINT (64-bit) holds up to ~9.2 quintillion. Use BIGINT for high-volume tables that could exceed 2B rows, or for Unix timestamps in milliseconds.

questions.prompt: A column stores 'active', 'inactive', 'pending' — three fixed states. What is the most semantically correct type choice?
options: TEXT with a CHECK constraint limiting values, or an ENUM type if the engine supports it
BOOLEAN — because there are only a few states
questions.answer: TEXT with a CHECK constraint limiting values, or an ENUM type if the engine supports it
questions.explanation: Text with a constraint (or ENUM) makes the allowed values explicit and enforced. INTEGER codes require a separate lookup to understand meaning. BOOLEAN only handles two states.
